content: Midwives are globally recognized as primary care providers for childbearing women. It is important to determine whether midwife continuity of care models differ in effectiveness compared to other care models. This review updates a previous analysis conducted in 2016. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of midwife continuity of care models with other care models for pregnant women and their infants. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as of August 17, 2022. Both published and unpublished randomized trials were included, where pregnant women were assigned to either midwife continuity of care models or other care models during pregnancy and childbirth. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion, scientific rigor, and risk of bias. Data extraction and analysis were performed, with primary outcomes including spontaneous vaginal birth, cesarean section, regional anesthesia, intact perineum, fetal loss after 24 weeks of gestation, preterm birth, and neonatal death. The GRADE system was used to evaluate the certainty of the evidence. Seventeen studies involving 18,533 women were included in the analysis. These studies were conducted in Australia, Canada, China, Ireland, and the United Kingdom. Most studies excluded women at high risk of complications, and three ongoing studies are focusing on disadvantaged populations. All included studies were deemed to have a low risk of scientific integrity concerns. Primary Outcomes: Midwife continuity of care models likely increase the rate of spontaneous vaginal birth from 66% to 70% (risk ratio [RR] 1.05, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03 to 1.07; moderate-certainty evidence). These models likely reduce cesarean section rates from 16% to 15% (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.84 to 0.99; moderate-certainty evidence). There is likely little to no difference in the rate of intact perineum (29% in other care models versus 31% in midwife continuity of care models; RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.12; moderate-certainty evidence). There may be little to no difference in preterm birth rates before 37 weeks of gestation (6% in both care models; RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.16; low-certainty evidence). The effect of midwife continuity of care models on the use of regional anesthesia is very uncertain (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.92; very low-certainty evidence). The impact on fetal loss at or after 24 weeks of gestation is also very uncertain (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.73 to 2.13; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the effect on neonatal death is very uncertain (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.71; very low-certainty evidence). Secondary Outcomes: Midwife continuity of care models likely reduce the rate of instrumental vaginal births (forceps or vacuum) from 14% to 13% (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.96; moderate-certainty evidence). These models may reduce the rate of episiotomy from 23% to 19% (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.91; low-certainty evidence). There is likely little to no difference in postpartum hemorrhage rates (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.03; moderate-certainty evidence). Admission rates to special care nurseries or neonatal intensive care units are also likely similar between the two care models (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.03; moderate-certainty evidence). There may be little to no difference in the rates of labor induction (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.00; low-certainty evidence), breastfeeding initiation (RR 1.06, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.12; low-certainty evidence), and low birth weight (<2500 g) (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.08; low-certainty evidence). The effect of midwife continuity of care models on thirdor fourth-degree perineal tears is very uncertain (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.49; very low-certainty evidence). Maternal readmission within 28 days is also very uncertain (RR 1.52, 95% CI 0.78 to 2.96; very low-certainty evidence). Attendance at birth by a known midwife is very uncertain (RR 9.13, 95% CI 5.87 to 14.21; very low-certainty evidence). The effect on Apgar scores ≤7 at five minutes is very uncertain (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.24; very low-certainty evidence). The impact on fetal loss before 24 weeks of gestation is very uncertain (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.01; very low-certainty evidence). No maternal deaths were reported in the three studies that assessed this outcome. However, the confidence in these findings is limited due to potential biases, inconsistencies, and imprecision in some estimates. Additionally, data were unavailable for outcomes such as maternal health status, neonatal readmission within 28 days, infant health status, and birth weight ≥4000 g. Women receiving care under midwife continuity of care models generally reported more positive experiences during pregnancy, labor, and postpartum. Cost savings were observed during the antenatal and intrapartum periods in these models. Conclusions: Women receiving midwife continuity of care were less likely to undergo cesarean sections and instrumental births and may be less likely to experience episiotomy. They were more likely to have spontaneous vaginal births and report positive experiences. However, the certainty of some findings is limited due to potential biases and inconsistencies. Future research should focus on the effects of these care models on women with social risk factors, those at higher risk of complications, and the implementation of these models in lowand middle-income countries.
